report:
## Conclusion

The evidence strongly supports your claim: bystander hands-only (compression-only) CPR is associated with significantly greater survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA) than no bystander CPR at all.

**Evidence base:**

1. **Randomized trials** (Sweden, US/DART, UK/OPALS-style dispatcher trials) comparing dispatcher-assisted compression-only vs. conventional CPR were designed to compare the two active interventions against each other, and both consistently outperformed no CPR historically; a meta-analysis of three such RCTs found compression-only CPR yielded modestly higher survival (~14% vs 12%) than standard CPR (https://www.ems1.com/research-monitor/articles/for-dispatcher-assisted-cpr-compression-only-may-be-best-NSEdFSCAsRKQZeIT/).

2. **Large observational studies**: A JAMA study (Bobrow et al.) found survival rose to 34% with compression-only CPR versus 18% for conventional/no CPR combined, referenced via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cardiopulmonary_resuscitation.

3. **Nationwide Japanese OHCA registries** (Iwami/Kitamura et al.) provide the strongest population-level evidence: bystander CPR (compression-only or conventional) was associated with markedly higher survival and better neurological outcomes than no bystander CPR, and dissemination of compression-only CPR training was linked to population-wide gains in favorable-outcome survival (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.112.109504; https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0140673610600645).

**Caveats:** Benefits are most pronounced for witnessed, cardiac-cause arrests in adults with short arrest duration; conventional CPR with rescue breaths may be superior for prolonged arrests, pediatric arrests, and non-cardiac (e.g., asphyxial) causes. Overall, though, hands-only CPR is a well-supported, evidence-based recommendation for adult bystanders.
